options: A simple gauge with only states and icons — no frame, scale, or pointer
A full chart with the legend removed
A type of dataset filter
A gauge that can only display text labels
questions.explain: Indicators and gauges both display a single data value, but indicators strip away the frame, scale, and pointer, leaving only states represented by icons.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the four built-in indicator sets?
options: Directional (up/down/flat arrows)
Logarithmic
Stacked
Nested
questions.explain: The four built-in indicator sets are Directional (trend arrows), Symbols (checkmarks/exclamation marks), Shape (traffic lights/signs), and Ratings (progressive icons like stars).

questions.q: Why are indicators especially well suited to tables and matrices?
options: Their simple icons stay legible even at small sizes
They automatically resize the entire table
They eliminate the need for a dataset
They can only be used inside tables, never standalone
questions.explain: Indicators' simple shapes make them effective even at the tiny sizes a table row or matrix cell forces on them — a full gauge's frame and pointer would be unreadable at that size.

questions.q: By default, how does an indicator decide which icon in its set to show for a given value?
options: Each icon owns a percentage range of the detected min/max, and the value's range determines the icon
The icon is chosen at random each time the report runs
Every value always shows the first icon in the set
Icons are assigned alphabetically by field name
questions.explain: By default, ranges are even percentage slices of the data's detected minimum and maximum — a five-icon set gets five 20%-wide bands — though every range can be edited explicitly.

questions.q: If you need to show a trend across multiple data points rather than a single current state, what should you use instead of an indicator?
options: A sparkline
A larger indicator icon
A second gauge panel
A report parameter
questions.explain: Indicators only ever represent one current value. To show multiple data points, such as a trend over time, use a sparkline instead.
